newsitem.title: USA: High-profile witnesses to emerge at secondhand-smoke trial.
newsitem.headline: High-profile witnesses to emerge at secondhand-smoke trial.

text.p: A former U.S. surgeon general and top tobacco executives will be leadoff witnesses for the 60,000 flight attendants whose landmark $5 billion secondhand smoke trial goes into high gear Monday, a plaintiffs' attorney says.
"We filed this (lawsuit) back in 1991, and finally we are getting to talk to a jury," attorney Stanley Rosenblatt said in a recent interview.

Rosenblatt -- who along with his wife, Susan, is pressing Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Inc. et al against seven tobacco companies and two trade groups -- will lay out his case Monday before a jury of four men and two women.

He said last week that on Wednesday he plans to call Julius Richmond, a U.S. surgeon general during the late 1970s under President Jimmy Carter. Rosenblatt declined to detail Richmond's testimony but said he expects to call another former surgeon general, Jesse Steinfeld, later in the trial.

Rosenblatt, who accuses the tobacco industry of conspiring to hide the health dangers of secondhand smoke, also said he expects to present on Wednesday a videotaped deposition of James Morgan, president of leading cigarette maker Philip Morris Inc.

Morgan was questioned by Rosenblatt for five or six hours in April, as were the chief executives of other tobacco companies named as defendants in the Broin case. Rosenblatt said he expects to present all the videotaped depositions during the trial, which is expected to last eight weeks or longer. Rosenblatt also said he expects later in the trial
to call as a witness Bennett LeBow, chief executive of Brooke Group, parent of cigarette maker Liggett Group, which is one of the defendants in the $5 billion lawsuit.

LeBow has been shunned by other tobacco company executives since Liggett made a private settlement with anti-tobacco forces credited with forcing the industry to agree to a historic $368.5 billion June 20 agreement with 40 attorneys general suing over health care spending on sick smokers.
Unlike the other chief executives of tobacco companies, LeBow lives in Florida and must respond to a Florida subpoena to appear in the trial, Rosenblatt said.

The dozen or so attorneys representing the tobacco industry declined to speak to reporters and have not detailed their defence, which is expected to challenge both the science linking lung cancer and other diseases with secondhand smoke and the charges of conspiracy and fraud.

An attorney for Philip Morris, David Hardy, said in court last week that he would not agree to allow the chief executives of the tobacco companies other than LeBow to be called by Rosenblatt. Hardy said the executives may appear later when the defendants present their evidence.
The tobacco lawyers, who deny any conspiracy and say the Broin class-action suit is legally wrongheaded and based on faulty science, are scheduled to present their opening statements Tuesday.

The plaintiffs, including American Airlines flight attendant Norma Broin, a 42-year-old mother whose lung cancer is in remission, were non-smokers and claim their tobacco-related diseases were caused by passengers' cigarette smoke aboard U.S. jets before 1988. Smoking was banned on U.S. domestic flights in 1988.
The Rosenblatts have said plaintiffs in the lawsuit could include up to 60,000 current and former flight attendants, but tobacco company attorneys have disputed that figure.
The Broin case is the first class-action claim against the tobacco industry and the first secondhand smoke case to go to trial in the United States. Jury selection in the case
lasted six weeks. Testimony in the Dade County court is expected to last through September or later before the jury gets the case.
